items.title: Coral reefs cover under 1% of the ocean but host around 25% of marine species
items.claim: What proportion of marine biodiversity do coral reefs support?

options.text: Around 25% of all marine species live on coral reefs, which cover less than 1% of the ocean floor — perhaps the most concentrated biodiversity hotspot on Earth
Coral reefs support only the species visible to divers

items.reveal:
Reefs occupy around 284,000 km² globally — under 0.1% of the ocean. The Great Barrier Reef is 2,300 km long. Species counts: around 4,000 fish species, 800 reef-building coral species, plus uncounted invertebrates.

Mass bleaching events (1998, 2010, 2014-17, 2024) have hit major reef systems. The Great Barrier Reef has experienced bleaching in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Some 50% of shallow corals on the GBR died in the 2016 event.

Reefs also provide coastal protection, fisheries and tourism value estimated at hundreds of billions of dollars annually.
items.why: Conservation priorities follow concentration. A small fraction of the planet holds an outsized share of biodiversity — losing reefs means losing whole ecosystems, not just iconic species.

items.title: El Niño returns roughly every 2-7 years
items.claim: What is the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)?

options.text: A single tropical storm in the Pacific
A coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation in the tropical Pacific recurring every 2-7 years; El Niño (warm central/eastern Pacific) and La Niña (cool) reshape global rainfall, drought and storm patterns
An annual cycle in the Arctic

items.reveal:
El Niño: weakened or reversed trade winds, warming of central and eastern equatorial Pacific, shifted convection. Typical effects: drought in Australia, Indonesia, parts of southern Africa; floods in coastal Peru and Ecuador; weaker Atlantic hurricane season; warmer global average.

La Niña: the opposite. The 1997-98 El Niño was among the strongest; 2015-16 contributed to record warm years and Great Barrier Reef bleaching.

Gilbert Walker first identified the Southern Oscillation atmospheric pattern in 1924 working with Indian Meteorological Department records. Jacob Bjerknes (1969) linked the atmospheric and oceanic components.
items.why: Global weather has oscillatory components. Forecasts months ahead are skilful when the ENSO state is known — and crops, water supplies and disaster planning across multiple continents depend on the call.

items.title: The Indian monsoon is driven by land-sea temperature contrast
items.claim: What causes the South Asian summer monsoon?

options.text: Differential heating: in summer the Asian continent (especially Tibetan Plateau) heats faster than the Indian Ocean, creating low pressure that draws in moist oceanic air; reversed in winter

items.reveal:
From June to September, the Tibetan Plateau (the world's largest elevated land mass) heats intensely; low-level winds reverse and blow from the southwest, drawing moisture from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal.

The Himalayas force orographic lifting, producing the wettest places on Earth: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (Meghalaya) regularly receive over 11,000 mm/year. The Western Ghats provide a similar barrier for the south.

Around 1.5 billion people depend on the monsoon. The Indian Meteorological Department's onset dates have varied by weeks recently. Climate change is shifting onset and intensity in ways that are not yet well predicted.
items.why: Monsoon variability is one of the highest-stakes climate signals on Earth. A failed monsoon means famine; a strong one means floods. The driver (differential heating) is testable physics but the year-to-year variability is poorly forecast.
